metaDescription: Six hammer drills and rotary hammers under $100 compared on motor, impact energy and chuck, with a clear view of what a budget tool gives up in concrete.
expertTake: The BLACK+DECKER BEHD201 is the best all-round budget hammer drill: a known brand, a 6.5-amp motor and a three-position side handle. The GALAX PRO 4.5-amp is the cheapest way to get any hammer action at all, and it is fine for a handful of anchor holes. For real concrete, skip the 1/2-inch hammer drills and take the DEKOPRO 12.5-amp SDS-Plus rotary hammer. Anyone drilling masonry once a year should rent or borrow a tool instead of owning one.
introParagraphs: A hammer drill is a drill with a pair of ratcheting discs inside that make the bit tap forward while it spins. That tapping chips masonry as the flutes clear the dust. At a low price the label can promise a lot, because blows per minute, amps and speed are easy numbers to print and hard to compare.
This guide explains what a budget hammer drill can and cannot do, which compromises are harmless for homeowners and which ones cost you time or bits.

products.name: BLACK+DECKER BEHD201 6.5-Amp 1/2 in Hammer Drill
products.description:
The BEHD201 is the textbook budget hammer drill. A 6.5-amp universal motor spins the chuck while two ribbed clutch discs ratchet against each other, which is where the 48,000 blows per minute figure comes from. The two-position switch sends you into plain drilling for wood and metal or hammer mode for brick and block.

Compared with the GALAX PRO at 4.5 amps it has about 44 percent more motor current behind the chuck, and that matters when you lean into a 3/8-inch masonry bit. It still sits well below the 9-amp Seesii and DEKOPRO rotary hammers, which strike with a piston instead of a ratchet.

The three-position side handle is the quiet feature, because it lets you brace the tool against the twisting kick when a bit binds on rebar or an aggregate stone. Ownership is simple. Blow dust out of the vents after masonry sessions, replace dull masonry bits before blaming the drill, and keep the hammer switch off for wood so the clutch discs do not wear for nothing.
products.bestFor: Homeowners who need an occasional anchor hole in brick or block and a decent drill for everything else.
pros: Handle swings to three positions for bracing
Name-brand parts and service availability
Strong enough for brick and block anchors
Simple two-position hammer switch
cons: Keyed-style limits on bit change speed

products.name: GALAX PRO 4.5-Amp Corded Hammer Drill with Bits
products.description:
The GALAX PRO is the cheapest machine in this lineup, and it behaves like one. A 4.5-amp motor spinning up to 3,000 RPM is a small-drill power budget with hammer clutch discs added, so you get the tapping action on a very low ticket. The metal keyed chuck is the sturdy part of the design, since a keyed chuck grips round and hex shanks without slipping when the hammer is running.

Next to the BEHD201 at 6.5 amps it gives up roughly a third of the motor current, and you notice it as stalls when a masonry bit meets an aggregate stone. The high 3,000 RPM top speed is useful for small wood and metal bits and a poor match for masonry, where you want slower, steadier rotation so the tungsten tip is not cooked.

If your plan is one shelf bracket and a clothesline anchor, this is the sensible way to spend as little as possible.
products.bestFor: Renters and occasional users who need a hammer function on the lowest possible budget.
pros: Lowest entry cost of the group
Metal keyed chuck grips bits firmly
12-speed control suits small bits
Light enough for overhead anchors
cons: Keyed chuck is slower to change

products.name: Hammerhead HAHD075 7.5-Amp 1/2 in Hammer Drill
products.description:
The Hammerhead is the middle step between the 6.5-amp BEHD201 and the 9-amp rotary hammers. A 7.5-amp motor, a variable-speed trigger and a keyless metal chuck make it feel like the drill many brands sell at twice the money. The keyless chuck is the real convenience here, because masonry work means swapping between a pilot bit, a masonry bit and a driver tip.

Its hammer mechanism is still the ratchet-disc design, so the 7.5 amps help with sustained boring and not with impact energy. Next to the Seesii SDS-Plus tool at 3 joules, it taps harder in no real sense, but it spins a 1/2-inch round-shank bit that the SDS tools cannot hold. That makes it the better single tool if you drill big holes in wood and occasional holes in brick.

Budget brands like Hammerhead are best bought for the first five years of light use. Keep the vents clear, do not let the motor run hot against a stuck bit, and stop if the smell changes.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want extra corded power for large wood holes and still want a hammer mode.
pros: 7.5-amp motor outpaces the other drill-style picks
Keyless chuck saves time on bit changes
Variable trigger controls starts on masonry
Six bits in the box for first jobs
cons: Ratchet hammer is mild in concrete

products.name: CRAFTSMAN V20 CMCD711C2 Cordless Hammer Drill Kit
products.description:
The CMCD711C2 is the cordless answer to the budget question, and it is the only battery tool in this roundup. The kit includes two batteries and a charger, so you can work while one pack charges. The 280 unit watts out rating is Craftsman's own power figure, which is a fair way to compare it with other Craftsman tools and an awkward way to compare it with brands that publish torque in inch-pounds instead.

Hammer action on a cordless tool eats the battery quickly, because the clutch discs add friction on top of the motor load. A 20V compact pack will drive a dozen or so anchor holes in brick, then it wants a rest. Against the corded BEHD201, you give up endless runtime in return for freedom from extension cords on a ladder or in a crawlspace.

The real purchase here is the V20 battery platform, which shares packs with a wide range of tools. If you already own V20 gear, the bare-tool value is excellent, and if you do not, the two batteries still make the kit a fair starter set.
products.bestFor: People who want a cordless drill and an occasional hammer function without buying separate tools.
pros: Two batteries and a charger in the box
Ratcheting chuck holds bits well
Cordless freedom on ladders and roofs
Shares packs with the V20 tool line
cons: Hammer mode drains the pack quickly
Weaker than corded in repeated masonry

products.name: DEKOPRO 12.5-Amp SDS-Plus Rotary Hammer
products.description:
The DEKOPRO is a different machine from the others, and the reason to buy it is the mechanism. A piston inside the tool pounds the bit's tail directly, delivering 5.5 joules per blow, which is far more concrete-breaking energy than a ratchet-disc drill can make. The SDS-Plus shank slides in the chuck so the bit hammers freely while it rotates.

At 12.5 amps it is the strongest tool in this lineup, ahead of the 9-amp Seesii at 3 joules by about 80 percent in impact energy.

The cost of power is size and the SDS bit requirement: a regular round-shank drill bit will not fit, so you buy SDS-Plus bits as well. Grease the chuck periodically, let the tool run to a stop before lowering it, and use a sharp bit, because a dull bit is the leading reason rotary hammers feel weak. If you hang more than a dozen anchors in concrete a year, this is the tool.
products.bestFor: Homeowners tackling a slab, a foundation wall or a patio project with real anchor counts.
pros: 5.5 J piston impact crushes concrete
Safety clutch protects your wrists
Chisel mode works for light demolition
12.5 amp motor holds speed under load
cons: Needs SDS-Plus bits and extra cost
Heavy and bulky for overhead work

products.name: Seesii 9-Amp SDS-Plus Rotary Hammer Drill
products.description:
The Seesii is the middle path between a hammer drill and a full-size rotary hammer. An 850-watt motor drives a piston mechanism that delivers 3 joules per blow, with 1,300 RPM and 5,500 blows per minute at the top end. The maker lists capacity of just over 1 inch in concrete, 1-3/16 inches in wood and 1/2 inch in metal, which is a believable homeowner range.

Next to the DEKOPRO it hits with roughly 55 percent of the energy, so each hole takes longer, but it is a lighter machine to hold overhead. Compared with the BEHD201, a real piston means fewer wasted seconds against hard aggregate. The four modes cover drill, hammer drill, chisel and a fixed chisel position for aiming a point or flat chisel.

Ownership caveats start with the SDS-Plus bit requirement and the thinner brand support. Use the side handle every time, keep the chuck greased, and watch the cord when drilling overhead.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want an SDS tool for light concrete work but not the weight of a heavy-duty machine.
pros: Piston mechanism beats ratchet-disc drills
Four modes include chisel positions
Lighter than the heavy rotary hammers
Respectable 1-in concrete capacity
cons: Brand support is thinner than major names

buyingCriteria.explanation: Budget hammer drills use two ratcheting discs, so the bit taps forward as the chuck spins. Piston rotary hammers instead strike the bit's tail with a free-flying piston and deliver impact energy in joules. A ratchet drill is fine for brick and block, but a rotary hammer is the only budget option that does real concrete. The BEHD201 and GALAX PRO use discs, while the Seesii at 3 J and DEKOPRO at 5.5 J use pistons.

Amps measure electrical draw, not power delivered, but within one tool type they track output. A 4.5-amp motor stalls in aggregate where a 7.5-amp one keeps going. Within the discs-only group, the GALAX PRO at 4.5 amps sits well below the Hammerhead at 7.5.

A 1/2-inch keyless or keyed chuck takes round and hex shanks, which means regular twist and masonry bits. SDS-Plus tools only accept SDS bits, and the bits cost more. Know before you buy what shanks you already own. If you also drill big holes in wood, the BEHD201 or Hammerhead is more flexible than the SDS-only Seesii or DEKOPRO.

Hammer action pulls the most current of any drilling mode. A cordless tool such as the CMCD711C2 will run a pack down after a dozen or so masonry holes. Corded tools give unlimited runtime for a fraction of the cost. For a basement full of anchor holes, plug in.

Masonry bits bind and the tool tries to spin in your hands. A side handle in multiple positions, as on the BEHD201, and a safety clutch, as on the DEKOPRO, are the two features that protect your wrists. Skipping them is the most common budget compromise that actually hurts.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Bit quality matters more than the drill
buyingCriteria.explanation: A dull or cheap carbide tip makes any of these tools feel weak. A sharp masonry bit in a GALAX PRO outperforms a worn one in a DEKOPRO. Budget around a few quality bits whenever you buy the drill.

specDecoder.meaning: The number of impacts the bit makes per minute. On a ratchet drill it is simply speed times the number of ridges on the discs, so a higher figure usually means a higher spin speed, not harder strikes.
specDecoder.watchFor: The BEHD201's 48,000 BPM and the Seesii's 5,500 BPM measure different things, so do not compare them directly.

specDecoder.meaning: Joules measure the energy per blow of a piston rotary hammer. More joules means each blow chips more concrete, which is why a 5.5 J tool outperforms a 3 J tool at the same speed.
specDecoder.watchFor: Ratchet drills do not publish joules because their strikes are mild, and a drill with no joule figure should not be bought for concrete.

specDecoder.meaning: Amps describe how much current the motor can draw. Within a tool type it points to sustained capacity, and a 7.5 amp drill will keep spinning in a bore where a 4.5 amp one stalls.
specDecoder.watchFor: Peak amp claims on lesser brands are sometimes overstated, so treat them as rough.

specDecoder.meaning: A shank system with grooves that lets the bit slide back and forth in the chuck. The bit gets the full hammer force without a clamping chuck absorbing it.
specDecoder.watchFor: The system only works with matching bits, and plain round shank bits will not fit.

specDecoder.meaning: A power rating of the Craftsman V20 line based on the watts delivered at the chuck, a proprietary figure. The CMCD711C2 is listed at 280.
specDecoder.watchFor: It cannot be compared with torque in inch-pounds or with other brands' ratings.

howWeEvaluated.title: Hammer mechanism and real capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: We separated ratchet-disc drills from piston rotary hammers first, because the two categories behave differently in concrete. Joule and amp figures were compared within the same type, with the DEKOPRO at 5.5 J and the Seesii at 3 J ranking above the disc-based BEHD201, GALAX PRO and Hammerhead for masonry.

howWeEvaluated.title: Chuck and bit compatibility
howWeEvaluated.description: A cheap tool is only useful if it accepts the bits you already own. We favored 1/2-inch chucks that accept standard shanks, and noted the SDS-only limits on the Seesii and DEKOPRO.

howWeEvaluated.title: Handle and safety features
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked for side handles, clutches and low-heat features that matter when a bit binds. The BEHD201's three-position handle and the DEKOPRO's safety clutch earned the most credit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Corded and battery runtime logic
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared corded tools with the CMCD711C2 cordless kit in terms of sustained hammer work, based on the spec sheet and owner feedback patterns about battery drain in masonry.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit for the budget
howWeEvaluated.description: Every tool here has a live price at or below the cap, and we ranked how much each one gives a homeowner for that money. The BEHD201 earned top overall for balanced capability and brand support, while the GALAX PRO earned the value badge for the lowest cost.

cards.label: Ratchet-disc drill
cards.text: Clutch discs tap the bit as it spins. They are light, hold ordinary round-shank bits and work well in brick, block and soft stone. The BEHD201, GALAX PRO, Hammerhead and Craftsman kit fall here.

cards.label: Piston rotary hammer
cards.text: A piston strikes the bit directly with 3 to 5.5 joules and uses SDS-Plus bits. It chews through concrete but cannot hold regular twist bits. The Seesii and DEKOPRO fall here.

howToChoose.note: Pick the ratchet drill if you also need a daily drill, and a rotary hammer if the main job is concrete.

howToChoose.subheading: Corded vs Cordless Within the Cap

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A piston mechanism with at least 3 joules, a side handle, a safety clutch and a sharp SDS bit. A ratchet drill can start a hole in concrete but will progress slowly and overheat.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The DEKOPRO's 5.5 J and clutch make it the concrete pick. The Seesii's 3 J is the lighter alternative. The BEHD201 is acceptable for a couple of holes in soft concrete only.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You drill masonry every month, need a long warranty or want to move up to a higher-brand rotary hammer. The DEKOPRO is the highest-spec tool at this cap, but a name-brand rotary hammer outlasts it.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You need one or two anchor holes. The GALAX PRO or BEHD201 covers that, and the Craftsman kit is useful if you also want a cordless drill.

maintenance.why: Masonry dust is abrasive and clogs the air path. A blast of compressed air or a brush keeps the motor cooler.
The bit slides in the chuck and wears it. A thin film of grease reduces wear.
Overhead drilling pulls on the cord. A frayed cord is a shock risk on a concrete floor.
A dull bit overheats the tool. Replace it before blaming the motor.
The Craftsman pack ages faster full or empty. Store it around 40 to 60 percent charge.

faq.q: Is a hammer drill good enough for concrete?
faq.a: A ratchet-disc hammer drill handles brick, block and soft concrete, but it is slow in poured slabs with hard aggregate. For more than a handful of holes, a piston rotary hammer is the better tool. The Seesii and DEKOPRO are the rotary options in this roundup.

faq.q: Can I use a hammer drill as a normal drill?
faq.a: Yes, by turning the mode switch to the drill symbol. The hammer action is off and the tool behaves like a corded drill. Leave hammer mode off for wood and metal to reduce wear.

The electric parts on cheaper brands are usually fine, but the support and parts are thinner. Look for double insulation, a firm switch and a sturdy cord. Replace the tool if the cord, switch or smell change.

BPM tells you how fast the discs strike, but a higher figure on a ratchet drill mostly reflects higher chuck speed. It does not tell you how hard each strike hits. Compare joules on rotary hammers instead.

faq.q: Do I need a dust mask for masonry drilling?
faq.a: Yes. Drilling concrete and brick throws crystalline silica dust, which is a lung hazard. Use a respirator rated for fine dust, eye protection and, where possible, a dust shroud or a vacuum held at the hole.

faq.q: Which of these suits a first-time buyer?
faq.a: The BEHD201 is the easiest start: familiar brand, simple switch and a three-position handle. If your plan is concrete, go straight to a rotary hammer, but expect to buy SDS bits too.
